sections.overview: The western marsh harrier is the largest of the harriers and a bird of reedbeds and marshes. In Britain it was extinct as a breeder in 1899, then recolonised from 1927 and has since recovered strongly.
sections.identification: A large, bulky raptor, larger and stockier than a hen harrier, with broad wings held in a shallow V when gliding. Adults average about 600 g; females are larger than males. The male is brown above and chestnut below, with tri-coloured wings of brown, grey and black tips. The female is chocolate brown with creamy patches on the throat and crown, and juveniles look much like her. There is no white rump, and the legs are yellow.
sections.habitat: It nests and hunts in reedbeds and marshes, and also uses farmland and open countryside. In England it breeds mainly in East Anglia, Somerset and the south-east, and is increasingly seen in winter around estuaries and marshes.
sections.diet: It flies low over the reeds and takes small waterbirds, small mammals such as rodents, and even frogs.
sections.behavior: In spring the male performs a sky dance, tumbling towards the ground and swooping back up; the female sometimes joins in, locking talons with him in mid-air. It is typically a migrant that returns to Africa in autumn, though many birds now winter in the UK.
sections.reproduction: There is typically one brood a year, of four or five eggs (observed range 3–10). The female incubates for roughly 31–38 days, and the downy chicks fledge at about 35–40 days. Breeding typically starts at three years of age.
sections.ecology: As a predator of small birds, rodents and amphibians, it sits near the top of the food chain in wetland habitats and depends on healthy reedbeds and marshes. A typical bird that reaches breeding age lives about six years; the oldest ringed bird reached over 13.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern. In Britain it fell to a single pair in 1971; BTO gives an estimated 590 breeding pairs in 2016, and the population rose by 271% between 1995 and 2024. RSPB cites about 700 pairs. It is Amber-listed in the UK and protected under Schedule 1 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act.
